name: ANGOLA

flag.title: Flag of Angola
flag.note: Red, black & a gold machete-star emblem

lead: Angola sits on Africa's Atlantic coast, roughly twice the size of Texas. It hides one of Africa's biggest waterfalls, a national animal so rare only 310 survive, and a dance — semba — that sailed the ocean and became Brazil's samba. After 27 years of civil war, skyscrapers now rise over Luanda's bay and Angola grows fast.

geo: Angola stretches from the Congo River basin in the north to the Namib Desert in the south — rainforest, savanna and sand dunes all in one country. The Kwanza River winds past elephant parks and fishing villages before emptying into the Atlantic.

In Malanje Province, black boulders called the Pedras Negras rise 200 metres above flat savanna. Nearby, Kalandula Falls — 105 metres tall, 400 metres wide — is a thundering curtain of water almost nobody outside Africa has heard of.
animals: Angola's national animal is the giant sable antelope — the palanca negra gigante — a jet-black bull with sweeping horns over 1.6 m long. It exists nowhere else on Earth. Civil war nearly wiped it out; only about 310 survive in two protected reserves.

Kissama National Park shelters elephants, hippos and crocodiles along the Kwanza River. In 2001, conservationists airlifted elephants in from Botswana by helicopter — one of Africa's most dramatic animal rescues ever.
culture: Angola gave the world a dance. Semba — a close, playful partner dance — was carried to Brazil and became samba. Back home, a smoother version called kizomba is now danced from Lisbon to Tokyo. Music fills markets, buses and every celebration.

Meals are built around funge, a thick cassava porridge scooped with your fingers, and moamba de galinha — chicken slow-cooked in red palm oil until golden. Guests are always offered food before any business is discussed.
history: The Kingdom of Kongo ruled northern Angola from the 1300s, trading ivory and cloth across Central Africa. When Portuguese ships arrived in 1483, the king welcomed them; his son Afonso I became one of Africa's first Christian monarchs.

Portugal colonised Angola for nearly 500 years. Independence came on 11 November 1975 — but civil war erupted the same day and raged until 2002. Twenty-four years of peace later, Angola is one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
wows: Kalandula Falls is Africa's 2nd-largest waterfall by volume — almost unknown outside the continent.
Brazil's samba traces directly to Angola's semba, carried across the Atlantic 400 years ago.
Half of Angola's population is under 16 — one of the world's youngest countries.
Scientists feared the giant sable extinct; in 2009 a bull was found and airlifted to safety.
Angola pumps over 1 million barrels of oil a day — the most in sub-Saharan Africa.
Landmines from the civil war are still being cleared; Princess Diana visited in 1997.
The Pedras Negras boulders are said to hold the footprints of warrior Queen Nzinga (1600s).

myths.myth: Angola is one of Africa's poorest countries
myths.fact: Angola is the 6th richest in Africa by GDP and its largest oil producer south of the Sahara, though wealth is unevenly shared.

myths.myth: Samba is purely a Brazilian dance
myths.fact: Samba grew from Angola's semba; the word comes from Kimbundu 'semba', a belly-bump move enslaved Angolans carried to Brazil.
